title: Emotional Intelligence · Episode 4
chapters: Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke
Self-compassion: being on your own side
How to really listen (and be heard)

units.t: Emotional Intelligence. Episode four.
In this episode: Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke, Self-compassion: being on your own side and How to really listen (and be heard).
Part one. Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke.
You got the job, passed the exam or won the award, and you're quietly waiting to be found out.
You are in very good company.
Waiting to be found out.
Picture a doctor newly qualified, a manager freshly promoted, or a student who topped the class.
From the outside they look confident.
Inside runs a different story: 'I got lucky.
Any day now, someone will realise I don't know what I'm doing.'
This feeling of being a fraud despite clear evidence of competence is widely known as impostor syndrome.
The concept was introduced in 1978 by American psychologists Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes, working with high-achieving women who credited luck or charm rather than ability.
Note the word phenomenon, not syndrome.
It is not a mental illness or a diagnosis.
It describes thoughts and feelings many ordinary, healthy people experience at times.
Later research found it in men as well, across many professions and cultures.
How common is it.
You may have seen claims that 70 per cent of people experience impostor feelings.
That figure is repeated often, but its origins are murky.
A 2020 systematic review led by Dena Bravata found reported rates from under ten per cent to over eighty per cent, depending on who was studied and how it was measured.
The honest conclusion is that nobody knows the exact figure, but impostor feelings are very common, particularly during transitions such as starting university, a new job or a promotion.
They seem especially frequent among people who are among the first in their family or community to reach a particular position, and in competitive fields where everyone around you seems brilliant.
The impostor cycle.
Clance described a self-sustaining loop sometimes called the impostor cycle.
Faced with a task, a person feels anxious and doubtful.
They respond in one of two ways: by overpreparing, working far longer than necessary, or by procrastinating, then working frantically at the last minute.
The task goes well.
But instead of concluding 'I'm good at this', they explain the success away.
If they overprepared, it was only the extra effort.
If they procrastinated, it was luck.
Either way, the success does not count as evidence of ability, so the doubt is ready and waiting for the next task.
Breaking the cycle often starts with noticing how you explain your wins, and whether you would accept that explanation from a friend.
Not a skill problem.
Impostor feelings are sometimes described as the opposite of the Dunning-Kruger effect, the idea that people with low skill overestimate themselves.
The comparison is catchy but loose.
People with impostor feelings are usually genuinely competent.
Expertise can even feed the feeling: the more you learn, the more you see how much you don't know, while beginners may be blissfully unaware of the gaps.
Some researchers also criticise the 'syndrome' label for putting all the focus on individuals.

If you are the only person like you in a room, hear subtle comments questioning whether you belong, or never see anyone with your background in senior roles, feeling out of place may be a reasonable response to real signals.
Leaders should ask what the environment is communicating, not just tell people to be more confident.
Quieting the inner critic.
Several simple habits loosen the grip of impostor feelings.
Talk about it: hearing that respected colleagues feel the same is powerfully reassuring.
Keep a record of positive feedback, results and things you have learned, and reread it when doubts flare.
Separate feelings from facts by asking, 'What evidence would convince me I'm competent?'
and checking whether it already exists.
Accept that not knowing everything is normal at every level.
Mentors can tell you what 'good' looks like in your field.
If self-doubt is persistent, affecting your sleep or mood, or stopping you from going for opportunities, it is worth speaking to your GP.
This is general information, not personal advice, and healthdirect and Beyond Blue have useful resources.
The key idea: Many capable people secretly believe they don't deserve their success, a pattern named in 1978 as the impostor phenomenon.
Part two. Self-compassion: being on your own side.
Many of us talk to ourselves in ways we would never talk to a friend.
Research suggests that harsh inner critic is not the motivator we think it is.
The inner critic.
Picture a friend who has just botched a job interview.
You would probably say interviews are nerve-racking, one bad day does not define them, and they will do better next time.
Now picture yourself in the same position.
Many people's inner voice says something like 'You idiot, you always choke.'
We tend to believe this harshness keeps us sharp, and that going easy on ourselves would make us lazy.
Psychologists who study self-compassion argue the opposite is often true.
Constant self-attack tends to make people more anxious, more afraid of failure and less willing to look honestly at their mistakes, which makes learning from them harder.
Three parts of self-compassion.
The modern science took off in 2003, when psychologist Kristin Neff defined self-compassion and built a way to measure it.
It has three parts.
Self-kindness means answering your own pain and failures with warmth, not harsh judgement.
Common humanity means remembering that struggle and imperfection are part of being human.
Mindfulness means noticing painful feelings clearly, without ignoring them or being swept away.
In short, treat yourself in hard moments as a good friend or coach would.
It is not self-esteem.
From the 1980s a self-esteem movement spread through schools, even a California task force in 1986.
A major 2003 review led by Roy Baumeister found that boosting self-esteem did little for school or work results.
Self-esteem often rests on judging yourself above average, so it collapses when you fail.
Self-compassion holds steady either way.
Kindness that motivates.
In 2012 psychologists Juliana Breines and Serena Chen, at the University of California, Berkeley, tested whether self-compassion breeds complacency.
Students sat a difficult vocabulary test designed so most would do poorly.
Afterwards some were encouraged to be understanding towards themselves, some got a self-esteem boost telling them they must be intelligent, and others got no message.
Offered the chance to study before a second test, the self-compassion group studied longer than either other group.
In other studies, people prompted towards self-compassion were more willing to take responsibility for a past wrong and try not to repeat it.
Kindness towards yourself seems to make facing your flaws feel safer.
What it is not.
Critics worry that self-compassion is a polite word for excuses.
It is not.
Self-pity dwells on how unfair life is to me in particular, the opposite of common humanity.
Self-indulgence grabs short-term comfort, like another night on the couch instead of training.
A compassionate response is often the tougher one: the good coach who says 'that hurt, it's understandable, now let's work out what went wrong.'
You can hold high standards and still speak to yourself decently.
Psychologist Paul Gilbert describes a threat system, a drive system and a soothing system.
Self-attack fires up the threat system, with racing heart, tension and urge to hide.
Self-compassion is thought to engage the soothing system.
Higher self-compassion is linked to lower anxiety and depression, though much of this research is correlational.
Practising it.
Self-compassion is a skill that improves with practice.
One simple method is the friend test.
When you notice a spiral of criticism, ask what you would say to a mate in the same situation, then say that to yourself, even if it feels awkward.

Neff suggests a short self-compassion break in tough moments that runs through her three parts: acknowledge that this is hard, remind yourself that others struggle with this too, and offer yourself a kind word.
Some people find a physical gesture helps, such as a hand on the chest.
Writing a letter to yourself from the point of view of a kind, wise friend is another exercise used in research.
None of this replaces professional help when you need it, but it is a good daily habit.
The key idea: Constant self-attack makes people more anxious and less willing to learn from mistakes, rather than more motivated.
Part three. How to really listen (and be heard).
Most arguments aren't about what they seem to be about.
Better communication starts with listening.
Listen to understand.
In most conversations we're waiting for our turn, planning a response or relating everything back to ourselves.
Author Stephen Covey put it simply: most people listen with the intent to reply, not to understand.
The other person can tell, and feeling genuinely heard is one of the most powerful things you can give someone.
Active listening is a set of simple skills.
Give full attention: phone away, eye contact, no interrupting.
Reflect back what you heard in your own words: 'So you're frustrated because you felt left out of the decision?'
Ask open questions starting with what, how or tell me.
And resist jumping in with solutions; people often want to be understood before they want advice.
Name it, own it.
Simply naming what someone seems to feel, like 'That sounds really stressful', tends to lower the temperature.
Brain-imaging research by psychologist Matthew Lieberman found that putting feelings into words reduced activity in the amygdala, a region involved in threat responses.
Validation says 'your feelings make sense', not 'you're right'.
When raising a problem, how you start matters.
'You never help around the house' is an attack, so the other person defends themselves.
An 'I' statement describes your experience instead: 'I feel overwhelmed when I do the dishes every night on my own.
Could we take turns?'
The formula: I feel [emotion] when [specific situation], because [why it matters].
Could we [request]?
It focuses on behaviour and needs, not character.
The four horsemen.
Psychologist John Gottman studied thousands of couples and identified four patterns he called the four horsemen, because they predict relationship breakdown.
Criticism attacks the person rather than the behaviour.
Contempt, including sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery, is the most damaging of all.
Defensiveness means making excuses and refusing responsibility.
Stonewalling is shutting down and withdrawing.
The antidotes: complain without blame, express appreciation, take responsibility for your part, and take a break to calm down.
Appreciation matters because Gottman found that stable couples have around five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict.
Take a break.
When an argument escalates, your heart rate climbs and your body floods with stress hormones.
In this state, called flooding, it's very hard to think clearly or listen, and people say things they regret.
Gottman's research suggests taking a break of at least 20 minutes and doing something calming, not rehearsing your arguments.
Agree on a time to come back to the issue.
Pausing isn't avoiding the problem; it gives both of you the chance to discuss it productively.
Feedback and small habits.
Feedback lands better when it's specific.
The Situation–Behaviour–Impact model is simple.
Describe the situation: 'In this morning's meeting…'.
Describe the specific behaviour, not your interpretation: '…you interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting…'.
Then the impact: '…and she didn't finish her point, so we missed her idea.'
Then ask for their view.
Give praise the same way; specific praise tells people what to repeat.
Small habits help too.
Keep your phone out of sight, since research suggests even a visible phone can make conversations feel less close.
Remember details people tell you.
And when you get it wrong, a sincere, specific apology without a 'but' goes a long way.
The key idea: Most people listen to reply; active listening means full attention, reflecting back and asking open questions.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is 'impostor phenomenon' the more accurate term than 'syndrome'?
Answer. It is a pattern of thoughts and feelings, not a diagnosis.
Question two. What do psychologists say about harsh self-criticism?
Answer. It tends to increase anxiety and fear of failure.
Question three. Which of these is a key part of active listening?
Answer. Reflecting back what you heard in your own words.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
